l: building of Demeter’s temple, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: After her revelation, Demeter orders a great temple and altar at Eleusis; Celeus gathers its people, who promptly complete them.

l: Chryseis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_awarded_to Agamemnon [as a prize from the spoils] Chryseis is taken among the spoils, and Agamemnon receives her as a prize. The Cypria is said to state that she had taken refuge at, or gone to, Hypoplacian Thebes to sacrifice to Artemis.

l: the pomegranate seed, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: binds Persephone [to return to the underworld] Hades secretly gives Persephone a sweet pomegranate seed, which she eats before leaving the underworld. Because she has tasted it, she cannot remain permanently with Demeter and must return below for part of each year.

l: seed, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: fails_to_sprout earth [during Demeter’s famine]

l: the famine, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: threatens mankind [with destruction] The famine is caused by Demeter’s grief and anger over Persephone’s absence. It threatens to destroy mankind and to end the gifts and sacrifices owed to the gods, but it ends when Persephone’s return is arranged.

l: Persephone’s seasonal return, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: occurs_in spring [when the earth blooms] Persephone returns to Demeter after Hermes brings her from the underworld. Because she has eaten the pomegranate seed, she spends two parts of the year with Demeter and the deathless gods and one part in darkness and gloom.

l: Athens, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Athens was the place to which Medea fled because she feared Creon's friends and relatives.

l: Cynthus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Cynthus is the rocky hill on Delos beside which Leto rests against a palm tree when she gives birth to Apollo. Apollo later walks upon craggy Cynthus.

l: Apollo’s temple, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo’s temple on Delos is promised to bring the island honor, crowds, hecatombs, and the continual savor of rich sacrifice. The hymn also says that Apollo has many temples and wooded groves in other places.

l: Apollo’s lyre, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo’s lyre is a high-pitched instrument with seven sheep-gut strings. Hermes makes it from a tortoise shell and other materials, tests its marvelous sound and sings with it, then keeps it by his cradle; Apollo later declares it always dear alongside his curved bow.

l: birth of Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo’s birth takes place on Delos after Leto swears that he will establish an altar, precinct, and oracle there. The goddesses wash and swathe him, Themis gives him nectar and ambrosia, and he immediately becomes too powerful to be held by cords or bands.

l: Leto’s labor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Leto suffers nine days and nine nights of extraordinary labor while Hera prevents Eilithyia from hearing of her trouble. Iris brings Eilithyia to Delos, after which the pains seize Leto and she gives birth.

l: Apollo’s arrival at Delos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo’s arrival at Delos follows Leto’s search for a willing land and the island’s acceptance of her promise. At his birth Delos rejoices, becomes covered with gold, and is chosen by Apollo as his dwelling above the other islands and shores.

l: Delian festival, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Delian gathering brings the long-robed Ionians, their children, and their wives together in Apollo’s honor. Boxing, dancing, song, and the performances of the girls of Delos form part of this celebrated assembly.

l: song and praise, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Song and praise are devoted to Apollo, Leto, and Artemis, and the girls of Delos sing about men and women of former times. Their songs imitate every human tongue so closely that each listener might think he himself were singing.

l: Apollo’s oracle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo’s oracle is a place of prophecy and divine counsel for people who question Apollo. Delos first seeks Apollo’s promised temple and oracle, but the oracle is established at Crisa, where Apollo offers unfailing counsel to visitors from many lands. Its responses guide Homer toward Ios and warn Hesiod of death at Nemean Zeus’s grove, though Hesiod misunderstands the warning.

l: old man and divine singer (in Colophon), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A blind, divine singer in Colophon, servant of the Muses and far-shooting Apollo, holds a lyre. Dwelling in rocky Chios, he is praised for supreme lays and named by Delian maidens as the sweetest singer at their gathering.

l: the poet-narrator, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: praises Apollo [continually] The poet-narrator praises Apollo, Leto, Delos, and the Delian maidens throughout the hymn. He asks the maidens to remember him and promises to carry their renown throughout the earth wherever he travels.

l: the dragoness, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A bloated, great, fierce she-dragon plagues mortals and sheep, raising Typhaon; Apollo kills her near a spring, where her sun-rotting body gives Pytho its name.

l: the Cretans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Cretans sail from Cnossos for trade, but Apollo carries them to Crisa; obeying him, they establish an altar and become temple ministers, guarding his oracle and righteousness.

l: Crisa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Crisa is the western-facing place beneath snowy Parnassus where Apollo decides to build his temple and oracle. The Cretan ship reaches its harbor, and the Cretans settle there as ministers of Apollo.

l: Ithaca, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_ravaged_by Telegonus Odysseus returns to Ithaca after Callidice’s death. Telegonus later lands there and ravages the island, prompting Odysseus to defend it.

l: the temple of Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo’s temple at Crisa, below Parnassus, is founded as an oracle; Trophonius, Agamedes, mortals, and countless people build its stone footing and structure for seekers’ offerings and counsel.

l: the Cretan ship, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo boards the Cretan ship in the shape of a dolphin and makes it tremble while the crew sails helplessly. He guides it past the coasts of Peloponnesus to Crisa, where it grounds on the shore.

l: Apollo’s journey in search of an oracle site, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A divine journey in which Apollo travels through many regions seeking an oracle site, ultimately choosing Crisa beneath snowy Parnassus for a temple.

l: the founding of the temple at Crisa, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo lays out the foundations of his temple at Crisa, and Trophonius and Agamedes set its stone footing. Human communities then build the temple of wrought stones so that it will be celebrated forever.

l: Apollo’s slaying of the dragoness, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo slays the dragoness near a sweet-flowing spring with an arrow, ending her plague of men and sheep, protecting mortals, and giving the place the name Pytho.

l: Apollo’s capture of the Cretans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a divine capture [by Apollo in dolphin form] Apollo captures the Cretans by leaping onto their ship in the form of a dolphin and directing its course to Crisa. He tells them that they will not return to Cnossos but will serve in his honored temple.

l: the Cretan foundation of Apollo’s sanctuary, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a foundation of a sanctuary [established by the Cretans under Apollo’s command] The Cretans found their service at Apollo’s sanctuary by hauling up their ship, making an altar, offering white meal, and following Apollo to Pytho. They become responsible for guarding the temple and receiving the people who gather there.

l: sacrifice, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_offered_to Apollo [at his altar and temple] is_required_at the temple of Apollo [as perfect hecatombs]

l: prophecy and divine counsel, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_provided_by Apollo’s oracle [as unfailing answers]

l: Muse, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Zeus’s clear-voiced daughter is invoked by Aphrodite and asked to sing of Aphrodite’s deeds and Mother of the Gods.

l: tortoise, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hermes finds a tortoise feeding near Maia's dwelling and treats it as an omen of good luck. He carries it inside, removes its limbs and marrow, and transforms its shell into the body of the first lyre.

l: the theft of Apollo's cattle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The theft of Apollo's cattle is committed by Hermes through trickery. On the day of his birth, Hermes steals the herd at night, reverses its tracks, drives it to Pylos, sacrifices two cattle, and conceals evidence and meat. Apollo follows the strange tracks, confronts Hermes, and, despite Hermes' denial, reaches a settlement after the cattle and cave evidence are recovered.

l: Hermes's invention of the lyre, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a invention [Hermes's] Hermes invents the lyre after finding a tortoise outside Maia's cave. He hollows out the shell, fixes reeds across it, stretches ox hide over it, adds horns and seven strings, and makes it sound through his playing.

l: the quarrel between Hermes and Apollo, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: concerns Apollo's cattle The quarrel begins when Apollo accuses Hermes of stealing his cattle. Hermes denies seeing or taking them, claiming that he is only a newborn concerned with sleep, milk, and swaddling clothes. Apollo calls him a rogue and robber, and the two continue disputing until they are brought before Zeus and the immortals.

l: the assembly on Olympus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_held_at Olympus [after the hour of gold-throned Dawn] The assembly on Olympus gathers after golden-throned Dawn. Hermes and Apollo are brought before the immortals, and the scales of judgment are set for them before Zeus.

l: the three prophetic sisters, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The three prophetic sisters are winged virgins dwelling beneath a ridge of Parnassus. They teach divination apart from Apollo: honey inspires truthful speech, while deprivation brings falsehood. Apollo grants Hermes access to their instruction.

l: the lyre, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_made_by Hermes [a marvellous musical instrument] The lyre produces marvelous music when Hermes plays it and sings while accompanying himself. Apollo is filled with wonder and longing for it, so Hermes gives it to him in exchange for Apollo’s whip and the office of cattle-keeping.

l: Hermes' golden staff, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo promises Hermes a splendid golden staff with three branches. It is to bring riches and wealth, protect Hermes, and help accomplish every task involving good words or deeds.

l: divination, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_known_by Apollo [fully and exclusively among the gods] Apollo refuses to teach Hermes the counsel of Zeus, declaring that only Zeus knows it. He nevertheless gives Hermes instruction through the three prophetic sisters and permits him to teach mortals their method when fortune favors them.

l: the exchange of the lyre and cattle-keeping, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: An event in which Hermes gives Apollo the lyre after its music is praised, and Apollo gives Hermes a shining whip and appoints him cattle-keeper, which Hermes accepts.

l: the oath of friendship, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The oath of friendship is sworn between Hermes and Apollo, confirmed by Zeus with an eagle. Hermes promises not to steal from or approach Apollo’s house; Apollo vows unmatched friendship, love, honor, gifts, and privileges for Hermes.

l: Trojans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Trojans receive Penthesileia and Memnon as allies, bury Penthesileia after Achilles kills her, and fight over Achilles’s body until Aias and Odysseus repel them. Later they debate the wooden horse, dedicate it to Athena, feast, and are attacked by Greeks.

l: love and sexual desire, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aphrodite spreads love and sexual desire among gods, mortals, birds, beasts, and other creatures. Zeus places desire for Anchises in her heart, and she in turn puts desire in the hearts of the animals accompanying her. Desire leads Anchises to sleep with Aphrodite despite believing that she is mortal.

l: marriage, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Marriage is refused by Hestia, who chooses to remain a maiden, while Aphrodite tells Anchises that Hermes has decreed that she will be his wedded wife. Aphrodite asks Anchises to present her to his family and prepare a marriage honorable among mortals and gods, though their union is instead concealed after she reveals her identity.

l: the encounter of Aphrodite and Anchises, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aphrodite goes to Mount Ida in the form of a mortal maiden and meets Anchises while he is alone and playing the lyre. Anchises believes her story that she is mortal, takes her to bed, and sleeps with her. Afterward Aphrodite reveals herself, and Anchises fears that lying with a deathless goddess will leave him weakened and miserable.

l: Aeneas’s birth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aphrodite says that she has conceived a child by Anchises and that the child will be called Aeneas. After he sees the light of the sun, mountain Nymphs will raise him, and he will become a godlike ruler among the Trojans.

l: old age, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_fated_for mortal men [harsh, deadly, and unavoidable] Old age is described as a harsh and deadly condition that eventually overtakes every mortal man and is dreaded even by the gods. Tithonus receives immortality but not freedom from aging, so he becomes unable to move or lift his limbs and is shut in a room. Aphrodite says that she would not want Anchises to live forever in such a state.

l: divine and mortal nature, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The unit contrasts deathless gods with mortal men, who are subject to old age and death. Aphrodite disguises herself as mortal but remains divine, while Anchises is mortal despite resembling the gods in beauty and stature. Their union produces Aeneas, whose divine and mortal ancestry makes him especially godlike among mortal men.

l: song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_ordered_by Aphrodite [as requested by the speaker] The speaker sings of Aphrodite and asks her to order the song. The speaker also says that another song will be remembered.

l: Tyrsenian pirates, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Tyrsenian pirates seize Dionysus for wealth, but his wonders drive them overboard, where they are transformed into dolphins.

l: the helmsman, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The right-minded helmsman recognizes a captive as possibly divine, urges release, receives Dionysus’s mercy and favor, and is made happy after Dionysus reveals himself.

l: the master, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a master [of the ship] The master rejects the helmsman's warning and orders the crew to continue sailing with Dionysus captive. When Dionysus appears as a lion, the lion springs upon the master and seizes him.

l: the ship, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A well-decked ship with mast and sail carries Dionysus and pirates across the sea, fills with wine and vine, and is abandoned by its crew.

l: the lion, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Dionysus becomes a dreadful lion in the ship's bows, roars and glares from the forepeak, then springs upon the master.

l: dolphins, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: are the transformed pirates The dolphins are the transformed pirates who leap overboard into the bright sea while escaping Dionysus's punishment.

l: the transformation of the pirates into dolphins, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_caused_by Dionysus [as divine punishment and escape from a miserable fate] When the pirates leap overboard to escape the lion and a miserable fate, they are changed into dolphins.

l: the pirates' capture of Dionysus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Tyrsenian pirates capture Dionysus on a shore and take him aboard, but their attempts to bind him fail as his bonds fall away.

l: war, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: War is associated with Ares's strength, spear-bearing power, and warlike Victory. The speaker asks for strength of war to drive away cowardice but also asks that violent strife and bloodshed be restrained.

l: song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The speaker sings of Cytherea and asks her to grant a cheerful song. The speaker also says that another song will be remembered.

l: people, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The people go out to war and come back. Pallas Athene saves them.

l: war, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: War is associated with deeds of war, the sack of cities, shouting, and battle. The people go out to war and return from it.

l: Mother of the Gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Mother of the Gods, mother of all gods and men, delights in rattles, timbrels, flutes, wolves, bright-eyed lions, echoing hills, and wooded coombes; the record ends with a speaker greeting her in song.

l: Eurystheus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a king Eurystheus commanded Heracles to wander over unmeasured tracts of land and sea and perform his labors.

l: Heracles' deeds of violence, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a deeds of violence [many] Heracles performed many deeds of violence while carrying out Eurystheus's bidding. He also endured many hardships during this time.

l: Dioscuri, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Dioscuri are the Tyndaridae, Castor and Polydeuces, children of Leda and Zeus. Born beneath Taygetus, they ride swift horses and aid men and ships in storms: appearing on tawny wings, they calm winds and waves, becoming signs of deliverance for shipmen.

l: Taygetus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a great hill Taygetus is associated with the heights beneath which stately Leda bore Castor and Polydeuces.

l: Pan, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Pan is a shepherd-god and dear son of Hermes, marked by goat’s feet, two horns, beard, and lynx-pelt. He roams wooded glades and mountain peaks, keenly hunts wild beasts, then at evening plays reed pipes, sings, and dances with nymphs. His merry noise and song delight the immortals’ hearts.

l: nymphs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Nymphs wander wooded glades and sheer cliff edges, dancing and singing with Pan beside dark water; clear-voiced and nimble-footed, they celebrate blessed gods, high Olympus, and Hermes.

l: song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Song accompanies Pan’s activities, as he plays his reed pipes and sings with the nymphs. The text’s song praises the gods, high Olympus, Hermes, and Pan, and it seeks Pan’s favor.

l: crafts, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Men learned crafts through Hephaestus, and these crafts enabled them to live peacefully in their own houses throughout the year.

l: house (Apollo's holy house), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Apollo's holy house stands at goodly Pytho, where Hestia tends it and is invited to enter.

l: song (the speaker's song), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The song is addressed through a request that Hestia bestow grace on it.

l: singers, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Singers exist upon earth through the Muses and Apollo.

l: kings, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: are_from Zeus Kings are said to come from Zeus.

l: song, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The speaker asks the Muses and Apollo to honor the speaker’s song. The speaker says that another song will also be remembered.

l: all creatures, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_in the world All creatures in the world, including those that walk upon the land, travel the paths of the seas, and fly, are fed from Earth's store.

l: harvests, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Harvests are among the blessings Earth grants to men. For men whom Earth honors, the fruitful land is laden with corn.

l: Moon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Moon, long-winged celestial body also called Selene, shines from heaven, embraces earth, brightens air, and reaches brightest fullness mid-month as a sign to mortals.

l: Pandia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Pandia, daughter of Selene and Zeus, is exceedingly lovely among the immortal gods.

l: shipmen, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Shipmen invoke Dioscuri during threatening storms, vow white lambs at the prow, then rejoice and rest when the storm is calmed.

l: ships, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Ships, swift-going, are submerged by wind and waves in stormy gales until Castor and Polydeuces appear and bring relief.

l: waves, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: are_on sea [at the surface] The waves of the sea can lay a ship under water during a storm. The Dioscuri still them upon the surface of the sea.

l: deliverance, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_from toil Deliverance is associated with the Dioscuri, who save men and ships from stormy seas. Their appearance is a fair sign and brings deliverance from toil.

l: The War of the Titans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The War of the Titans is an uncertainly attributed work containing traditions about Heaven, Earth, Aegaeon, the Titans, Zeus, Cronos, Cheiron, Heracles, and the apples of the Hesperides, beginning with these traditions and including Heracles sailing across the sea in a cauldron.

l: Aegaeon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aegaeon, son of Earth and Sea, dwells in the Sea and is an ally of the Titans.

l: Story of Oedipus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Story of Oedipus is Cinaethon’s 6,600-verse epic, recounting Oedipus’s sons’ birth to Euryganeia and the Sphinx’s killing of Haemon.

l: Iocasta, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Iocasta is said not to have had children by Oedipus in the account cited by Pausanias.

l: Euryganeia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Euryganeia was the mother of Oedipus’s sons according to the Story of Oedipus.

l: the sons of Oedipus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The sons of Oedipus, born of Euryganeia, are cursed after actions involving their father, then assigned war and fighting, fall by one another’s hands, and go into Hades.

l: Creon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: rules Corinth [at that time] Creon was the ruler of Corinth when Medea poisoned him. After his death, his relatives killed Medea's sons and spread the story that Medea had killed both them and Creon.

l: Haemon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Creon’s noble, lovely son, Haemon, is described affectionately before the Sphinx kills him.

l: The Thebaid, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: An epic of seven thousand verses begins by singing of parched Argos, unfolds through Oedipus's curses, Adrastus's flight, battle and Parthenopaeus's death, ending with seven dead buried.

l: war and fighting between the sons of Oedipus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_the_portion_of the sons of Oedipus [ever] Oedipus prayed that war and fighting would always be the portion of his sons rather than their sharing their father's goods in loving brotherhood. He also prayed that each would fall by the hand of the other.

l: Epigoni, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Epigoni is an epic poem attributed to Homer, seven thousand verses long, beginning by invoking the Muses to sing of younger men.

l: Teumesian fox, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Sent by the gods to punish Cadmus’s descendants, it leads Thebans to exclude Cadmus’s house from kingship.

l: hound, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: escapes_no_beast no beast Cephalus's hound was said to be able to catch every beast. It overtook the Teumesian fox, and it was then turned into a stone along with the fox near Teumessus.

l: Procris, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_killed_by Cephalus [accidentally] Procris was the wife of Cephalus. Cephalus accidentally killed her and was subsequently purified of the homicide by the Cadmeans.

l: Epigoni (the victorious descendants), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: send Manto [to Delphi as a first fruit of their spoil] The Epigoni sent Manto to Delphi as a first fruit of their spoil. An oracle of Apollo directed her to marry the man she met, who was Rhacius.

l: Rhacius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Rhacius, son of Lebes and Mycenaean by race, meets and marries Manto in accordance with Apollo's oracle.

l: Colophon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: claims_as_associated_with Homer [as the place where he began composing] Manto came to Colophon after marrying Rhacius. There she was much cast down and wept over the destruction of her country.

l: hunting of the Teumesian fox, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Cephalus hunts the Teumesian fox with his hound after purification for killing Procris; they overtake each other and become stones near Teumessus.

l: transformation of the hound and fox into stones, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The hound overtakes the Teumesian fox near Teumessus, and both transform into stones.

l: The Cypria, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Cypria is an eleven-book epic, attributed variously to Stasinus, Hegesias, or Homer, recounting Zeus’s plan with Themis and mythological details through the early Greek campaign against Troy.

l: Alexandrus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Alexandrus judges Aphrodite fairest for promised marriage with Helen, sails from Troy to Sparta, carries Helen and treasures away, takes Sidon, and returns to celebrate marriage.

l: Helenus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a prophet [concerning the taking of Troy] Helenus is captured by Odysseus. He prophesies what is required for the taking of Troy, leading to Diomedes’ bringing Philoctetes from Lemnos.

l: Cassandra, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_connected_to image of Athena [Aias tears it away while dragging her] Aias the son of Ileus tries to drag Cassandra away by force. In doing so, he tears away the image of Athena with her.

l: Sparta, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Sparta is where Menelaus entertains Alexandrus and where Alexandrus gives gifts to Helen. Helen later leaves Sparta with Alexandrus while Menelaus is away.

l: Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Ilium is a city targeted by Menelaus and his allies, who first fail to land and later demand Helen and treasure. After its people bring in a wooden horse, Greeks enter, signal their attack, capture and burn the city, kill Priam and Astyanax, take Andromache, and divide its inhabitants and treasures.

l: Greek expedition against Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_led_by Menelaus [with Agamemnon] The Greek expedition against Ilium is planned by Menelaus and his brother and assembled by gathering leaders across Hellas. It musters at Aulis, mistakenly sacks Teuthrania, is scattered by a storm, reforms, and eventually sails toward Ilium.

l: Palamedes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Palamedes exposes Odysseus’s feigned madness by seizing Telemachus, then is drowned while fishing by Odysseus and Diomedes.

l: Briseis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_awarded_to Achilles [as a prize from the spoils] Briseis is taken among the spoils of the cities attacked by Achilles and is awarded to him as a prize.

l: Penthesileia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Penthesileia, Ares's Thracian Amazon daughter, aids Troy, fights greatly, is killed by Achilles, and buried by Trojans.

l: the body of Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: After Achilles is killed, Aias carries his body to the ships while Odysseus drives off the Trojans. The Achaeans lay it out, and Thetis later takes it from the pyre and transports it to the White Island.

l: Achilles’ arms, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Achilles’ arms, disputed by Odysseus and Aias, are awarded to Odysseus through Athena’s contriving and later given to Neoptolemus.

l: the arrival of Penthesileia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Penthesileia arrives to aid the Trojans and demonstrates great prowess before Achilles kills her.

l: the killing of Penthesileia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Achilles kills Penthesileia after she comes to aid the Trojans. The Trojans bury her, and Achilles is later criticized by Thersites for what is described as his supposed love for her.

l: the battle between the Achaeans and Trojans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Achaeans and Trojans fight after Memnon arrives to aid Troy. During the fighting, Memnon kills Antilochus, Achilles kills Memnon, and Achilles later routs the Trojans.

l: the death of Antilochus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Antilochus is killed by Memnon. The Achaeans bury him afterward.

l: the death of Memnon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Memnon is killed by Achilles after killing Antilochus. Eos then obtains immortality for Memnon from Zeus.

l: the death of Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Achilles is killed by Paris and Apollo after routing the Trojans and rushing into the city with them.

l: the struggle for Achilles's body, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A great struggle takes place over Achilles's body after his death. Aias carries the body to the ships, while Odysseus drives off the Trojans.

l: the funeral of Achilles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Achaeans lay out Achilles's body, while Thetis and the Muses bewail him. Thetis takes him from the pyre and transports him to the White Island; the Achaeans then pile a cairn and hold games in his honour.

l: the dispute between Odysseus and Aias, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A dispute arises between Odysseus and Aias over the arms of Achilles.

l: Aias’s suicide, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: occurs_at dawn [about] Aias kills himself about dawn.

l: Epeius, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: builds wooden horse [by Athena’s instruction] Epeius builds the wooden horse by Athena’s instruction.

l: wooden horse, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The wooden horse holds the Achaeans’ best men. After Achaean forces sail to Tenedos, Trojans take it into Ilium, debate it, dedicate it to Athena, and feast; hidden Greek warriors emerge and attack them.

l: Priam, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_at Zeus Herceius [at the altar when Neoptolemus kills him] Priam flees to the altar of Zeus Herceius during the sack of Ilium. Neoptolemus kills him there.

l: Astyanax, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Astyanax, son of Hector, is killed during the sack of Ilium, hurled from a tower or city wall by Neoptolemus or Odysseus.

l: Andromache, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Hector’s wife is taken by Neoptolemus as a prize after the Greeks sack Ilium.

l: storming of Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The storming of Ilium begins when the Greeks hidden in the wooden horse come out and the Achaeans arrive from Tenedos. Many enemies are killed, and the city is captured.

l: Aias the son of Ileus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Aias, son of Ileus, seizes Cassandra and Athena’s image during the sack of Ilium, escapes Greek stoning at Athena’s altar, and dies in a storm at the Capherides.

l: burning of Ilium, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_carried_out_by Achaeans [after the city was stormed] The Greeks burn Ilium after storming and capturing the city.

l: Polyxena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_sacrificed_at tomb of Achilles [by the Greeks] The Greeks sacrifice Polyxena at the tomb of Achilles after burning Ilium.

l: departure of the Greeks, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_followed_by Athena's plan to destroy the Greeks [on the high seas] After burning Ilium, sacrificing Polyxena, taking captives, and dividing the spoils, the Greeks sail away. Athena plans to destroy them on the high seas.

l: Penelope, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_married_to Telegonus [after Odysseus’s death] Penelope is transported with Odysseus’s body and Telemachus to Telegonus’s mother’s island. Circe makes her immortal, and Telegonus marries her.

l: Agamemnon's murder, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a murder Agamemnon’s murder is committed by Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra. Orestes and Pylades subsequently take vengeance for it.

l: Thesprotis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Thesprotis is where Odysseus goes after performing the sacrifices ordered by Teiresias. Its queen, Callidice, marries Odysseus, and its forces are led by Odysseus in a war against the Brygi.

l: killing of Odysseus by Telegonus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a killing [unwitting] Telegonus kills Odysseus unwittingly when Odysseus comes out to defend Ithaca from the ravaging of the island. Telegonus learns his mistake afterward and transports Odysseus’s body to his mother’s island.

l: mother's island, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Telegonus transports Odysseus’s body, Penelope, and Telemachus to his mother’s island. Circe makes them immortal there.

l: Expedition of Amphiarus to Thebes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Expedition of Amphiarus to Thebes, about Amphiarus, goes to Thebes and was among works Homer recited in the tanner’s yard.

l: The Taking of Oechalia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Taking of Oechalia concerns Eurytus, his daughter Iole, and Heracles, includes Medea's actions in Corinth and Athens, and is attributed either to Homer or Creophylus of Samos.

l: Oechalia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_sacked_by Heracles [for the sake of Iole] Oechalia was sacked by Heracles for the sake of Iole.

l: Iole, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Iole, also called Ioleia, was Eurytus's daughter. Heracles sacked Oechalia for her sake.

l: Creophylus of Samos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Creophylus of Samos reportedly hosted Homer and was linked to The Taking of Oechalia, either receiving its attribution from Homer or writing it under Homer's name; he also recounts Eurytus's sons and Medea's actions.

l: sacking of Oechalia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The sacking of Oechalia was carried out by Heracles for the sake of Iole, the daughter of Eurytus.

l: Phocais, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Homer composed the Phocais while living with Thestorides. The Phocaeans say that he composed it among them.

l: Phocaeans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: say Phocais [they say Homer composed it among them] The Phocaeans say that Homer composed the Phocais among them.

l: Margites (character), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Margites is a well-grown man who knows many things badly and fails at every craft, having been taught by the gods neither digging, ploughing, nor any other skill. He does not know whether his father or mother gave him birth. Married, he will not lie with his wife because he fears she will give her mother a bad account of him.

l: Cercopes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Cercopes are two brothers, Passalus and Acmon, children of Theia and Ocean. Accomplished knaves, liars, and cheats, they live on earth and continually roam the world deceiving men, until they are turned to stone for trying to deceive Zeus.

l: Passalus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Passalus, one of the Cercopes and Acmon’s brother, practised deceit and knavery with him, then was said to be turned to stone for trying to deceive Zeus.

l: Acmon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Acmon, one of the two brothers called the Cercopes, practised deceit with Passalus and was said to become stone after trying to deceive Zeus.

l: The Battle of Frogs and Mice, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: A one-day war begins when Puff-jaw abandons Crumb-snatcher; revenge-seeking Mice battle Frogs until crabs drive the Mice into flight at sunset.

l: Mice, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Mice, a race of people, fear ferrets, hawks, and traps. Enraged by Crumb-snatcher’s drowning, they arm for war against Frogs but flee when crabs attack.

l: Frogs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Frogs, a people living in and around the lake and ruled by Puff-jaw, gather against him, arm to fight the Mice, suffer heavy losses, and are rescued when Zeus sends crabs.

l: Crumb-snatcher, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Crumb-snatcher is a Mouse, king and warrior, son of Bread-nibbler and Quern-licker. He prefers human food, avoids vegetables, and fears ferrets, hawks, and traps. Riding Puff-jaw, he is drowned when Puff-jaw dives from a water-snake. He later fights for dead Mice, kills Leeky and Cabbage-climber, and is killed by Croakperson.

l: Puff-jaw, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Puff-jaw, child of Mud-man and Waterlady, is king of the Frogs. He invites Crumb-snatcher aboard, abandons him to drown when a water-snake appears, urges war on Mice, and is struck by Bread-nibbler.

l: the lake, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a body of water [inhabited by Frogs] The lake is where Crumb-snatcher drinks, rides with Puff-jaw, and drowns after Puff-jaw dives away. It becomes the setting for much of the battle, and its water is dyed with the blood of fallen fighters.

l: Bread-nibbler, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Bread-nibbler, Crumb-snatcher's father, mourns sons lost to ferret, human trap, and Puff-jaw; enraged by Crumb-snatcher's death, he arms the Mice and strikes Puff-jaw.

l: Slice-snatcher, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Slice-snatcher, strongest Mouse and Gnawer’s son, arms himself with split chestnut husks and threatens the Frogs, driving them toward the lake until Zeus intervenes.

l: the ferret, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: preys_on Mice [as a dangerous foe] The ferret is a dangerous enemy of the Mice. It has killed one of Bread-nibbler's sons and is feared because it can follow a Mouse into its hole; the Mice also make breastplates from the skin of a ferret they have flayed.

l: crabs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Crabs are mailed, shell-covered warriors with curving claws, eight legs, feelers, and backward-looking eyes; Zeus sends them to aid Frogs by attacking Mice, nipping their tails, paws, and feet until they flee.

l: the armor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: The Mice's armor consists of green bean-pod greaves, ferret-skin breastplates stretched on reeds, lamp-centre shields, bronze needle spears, and pea-nut helmets. The Frogs use mallow leaves for greaves, beet- and cabbage-leaf breastplates and shields, rush spears, and snail-shell helmets.

l: Pythia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: identifies_country_of Homer [in an oracle delivered during Hadrian’s reign] The Pythia gave several responses concerning Homer, identifying him in one response with Ithaca, Telemachus, and Epicasta, and warning him in another that Ios would receive him dead and that he should beware the riddle of young children. She also foretold Hesiod’s fame and warned him against the pleasant grove of Nemean Zeus.

l: Ios, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Ios was identified by an oracle as Homer’s mother’s country and as the place that would receive him dead. Homer eventually traveled there, stayed with Creophylus, died after falling in a clayey place, and was buried there.

l: Homer-and-Hesiod contest, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: At Chalcis in Euboea, Homer and Hesiod compete through questions, riddles, calculations, moral answers, and recitations. Though Homer excels in the exchanges, Paneides awards Hesiod the prize for promoting peace and husbandry over war and slaughter.

l: Homer's death, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: is_a death of Homer [on Ios after the fishing-riddle episode] At Ios, Homer asked boys returning from fishing what they had caught, but they answered with a riddle about catching lice. When he understood the riddle and connected it with the oracle, he composed his own epitaph, slipped in a clayey place, and died three days later.

l: Hesiod's works and agrarian teaching, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: advocates peace and husbandry [in contrast with Homer’s war poetry] Hesiod recited verses describing the proper seasons for harvesting, ploughing, and sowing, and the need to work according to the seasons. Paneides preferred this teaching about peace and husbandry to Homer’s depiction of warfare.

l: poetic composition and performance, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica
s: Poetic composition and performance is practiced by Homer and Hesiod through traveling recitation, public competition, epic verse, and agrarian moral teaching, culminating in Hesiod’s contest victory and tripod dedication.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The document is a collection of Pindar’s victory odes, Olympian, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian, followed by fragments of other song types. Its central purpose is to celebrate athletic victors, their families, cities, patrons, gods, and inherited renown. The poems repeatedly present victory as the product of personal excellence, training, wealth and generosity, divine favor, and public song, which preserves fame beyond a single contest. The Olympian odes begin with Hieron of Syracuse’s horse-race victory through Pherenikos and the myth of Pelops, rejecting the tale that Tantalos served Pelops to the gods. They honor figures including Theron of Akragas, Psaumis of Kamarina, Agesias, Diagoras of Rhodes, Alkimedon, Epharmostos, Agesidamos, Ergoteles, Xenophon, and Asopichos. These songs connect individual triumphs to cities, ancestors, gods, and myths such as Herakles’ founding of the Olympic games. The Pythian odes again prominently honor Hieron, as well as Arkesilas of Kyrene, Xenokrates, Megakles, Aristomenes, Telesikrates, Hippokleas, Thrasydaios, and Midas. Their narratives range through Typhon, Ixion, Asklepios, Jason and Medea, Perseus, and Orestes. They also offer counsel on truthful rule, moderation, repaying favors, political restoration, mortality, and the instability of fortune. The Nemean and Isthmian odes celebrate many victors, especially men of Aigina and Thebes, including Chromios, Timodemos, Aristokleides, Timasarchos, Pytheas, Alkimidas, Sogenes, Deinis, Theaios, Aristagoras, Herodotos, Melissos, Phylakidas, Strepsiades, and Kleandros. Aigina’s Aiakid lineage, Aiakos, Peleus, Telamon, Achilles, and Aias, recurs strongly, alongside Herakles and other heroic stories. Several poems warn against envy, slander, excess, tyranny, and ambitions beyond mortal limits. The closing fragments classify Pindar’s remaining work and preserve songs for Dionysos, Delos, and Thebes, plus dirges describing the blessed dead, judgment, atonement, and the survival of a shadow of life after bodily death. The document ends with “THE END.”

l: Hieron of Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Hieron of Syracuse is presented as a king, chief, captain, and leader of the Syracusans who rules Syracuse, Ortygia, Sicily, and Aitna with a sceptre of justice, righteous counsel, and benevolence. Favored by destiny, he possesses wealth, wisdom, military valor, generosity, and excellence in many forms; he treats citizens and strangers like a father. His rule includes founding Aitna near Etna, leading the Syracusans before Cumae and defeating the Etruscans, and protecting the Epizephyrian Lokrians from war. He is repeatedly celebrated in the Muses’ song for athletic victories: an Olympic horse-race with Pherenikos and Pythian chariot-races, including a four-horse car. The records portray his renown as joining political power, just governance, military protection, religious honor, and victories made enduring through song.

l: Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Pindar is a poet, author, composer, and singer of victory odes: a friend of winners in the games whose songs illuminate their cities, recall their achievements, and seek the Muses’ power to celebrate them. He praises Zeus and rejects the story of Pelops’ ivory shoulder because it would accuse the gods of an infamous act; he warns that beautiful but untrue tales do not endure. He also expresses ideas about future life and seems influenced by Pythagoreanism. His work unfolds through praise and promised repayment. He celebrates Epharmostos’ wrestling victories. After admitting he had forgotten a promised strain for Agesidamos, he pledges a longer celebration in Agesidamos’ Italian home and composes a victory song for Agesidamos and the Lokrians. He sings for Hieron of Syracuse, praising Hieron’s victories and city and comparing his own praise to a javelin thrown beyond rivals. From Thebes he sends an ode to Syracuse, honoring Hieron’s valor, wealth, wisdom, and directness while condemning flattery, slander, bitterness, and crooked conduct. He composes for Arkesilas’s chariot victory. At twenty, in what is identified as his earliest entire surviving poem, he praises Hippokleas, his family, and Thessaly. He writes for Herodotos of Thebes, postponing an intended song for Apollo to celebrate Herodotos, Asopodoros, Thebes, and hoped-for future crowns. Finally, he comes from the house of Zeus with a bright song for Bromios, attends the Nemean games in winter, and foresees approaching spring and the vernal Dionysia from tokens of a branch.

l: Olympic games, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The Olympic games are the greatest among games, sacred to Zeus and praised as a source of glorious hymn, lasting fame, and sweet tranquillity for winners. Tradition connects their founding both to Pelops and to Herakles, who established them beside the ancient tomb of Pelops after sanctifying altars to his sire. The ordinance of Herakles is held at Pisa, in its famous valley beside the Alpheos, as a fifth-year feast in the middle of Hekatombaion, at the full moon. Elean truce-bringers proclaim the games with a universal truce, and a judge presides. Contests begin with foot-racing and wrestling and include boxing, javelin, stone-throwing, chariot-racing, and the four-horse chariot race. Competitors such as Diagoras, Asopichos, and Theaios gain praise or victory there; winners receive wreaths and garlands, and their success is carried into customary hymns and ode.

l: Sicily, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Sicily is a teeming land, given by Zeus to Persephone and intended for exaltation as the best in the fruitful earth, crowned with citadels. It includes Akragas and warlike people, and becomes Ergoteles’s adopted homeland after he leaves Crete and is naturalized at Himera.

l: Pherenikos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Pherenikos is Hieron of Syracuse’s winning horse. Running ungoaded beside the Alpheos, he wins the horse-race at Pisa and Olympia; he also wins the Pythian contest at Kirrha. His victories bring glory to Hieron and supply the splendour of his Pythian crown.

l: Pisa, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Pisa is a place, a colony of Lydian Pelops and an abode of Zeus, containing Altis and a famous valley for games. There Pherenikos wins the horse-race and Pelops’ Olympian contests occur; it bids divinely assigned song for victors. After victories, Herakles gathered host and booty there and established grove and games’ arrangements.

l: Pelops, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Pelops, loved by Poseidon and created by Klotho with an ivory shoulder, is returned by the immortals to the short-lived race of men. After reaching youth, he defeats Oinomaos to marry Hippodameia; they have six sons. He is honored by a tomb beside the Alpheos, while the Olympic games are founded beside that tomb by Herakles.

l: Poseidon, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Poseidon is a god: the Bright Trident, Wielder of the Trident, wide-ruling god of sea and horses, earth-shaking son of Kronos, and earth-grasper. He devises horses and chariots, rules Isthmos, and is deity, inhabitant, and divine patron of the Isthmus of Corinth. He loves Pelops, carries him to Zeus’s house in Olympus, and later answers Pelops’s call with a golden car and winged, untiring steeds, enabling victory over Oinomaos. Through Pitane and Euadne, he is Iamos’s grandsire; Iamos calls on him, and a poem asks him for safe voyage and blessing. During the Argonauts’ voyage he is invoked as lord of the sea and receives a shrine near the Axine sea. He restores the Kleonymid house’s glory through a hymn and grants calm after grief. He desires Thetis, but an oracle warns that her son would surpass his father.

l: Tantalos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Tantalos, father of Pelops, hosted and was exceptionally honored by the gods at beloved Sipylos. His excess and wrongdoing ended that fortune: he stole nectar and ambrosia from the immortals for mortals, and the gods punished him with a great stone hanging above his head.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Zeus is an Olympian, eternal god: son of Kronos and Rhea, husband of Hera, king of heaven and the immortals, lord of Olympus, Olympia, and the Olympic games. He dwells above clouds on the Kronian hill and is marked above all by thunder, white, red, and bickering lightning, through which he gives signs, confirms prophecies, stops expeditions, kills or buries opponents, and governs events. His authority extends over human fortune, excellence, fame, prosperity, laws, and the outcomes of things; he can humble pride, sustain those who honor him, and protect cities, lands, families, and victors. The records repeatedly present him as the god of athletic worship and victory. Sacred groves, altars, libations, ordinances, crowns, and songs at Olympia and Nemea belong to him. Petitioners ask him to preserve honor, grant prosperity and old age, protect Aigina, Corinth, Kamarina, Aitna, and other places, and make victories renowned. He is also associated with music and poetry and is invoked by bards. Zeus's family is extensive. He fathers Athene, Semele, Achilles, Lokros, Epaphos, Herakles, Aiakos, Polydeukes, and others; he is ancestor of the Aiakidai and connected with Aigina, Peleus, Telamon, and Achilles. He grants Polydeukes a choice involving Kastor, answers Herakles’ prayer, and promises Peleus a sea-bride. His actions include raining gold on Rhodes, giving Sicily to Persephone, causing and ending a flood, ordaining destinies, and defending or favoring communities. From his origins as Kronos’s son, the account unfolds through his cosmic rule, kinship, judgments, benefactions, and continuing worship as the powerful source of victory, order, and human fortune.

l: gods, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Gods, born from Earth with men, eat at Tantalos’ table and would be guilty if its legend were accepted; aided by Graces, they rule feast or dance and fight giants at Phlegra.

l: gods, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: may_accomplish bliss [for mortal men, even today] They are worshiped with incense of every kind upon altars. A shadow of life comes from them.

l: Hippodameia, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_daughter_of Oinomaos [the Pisan father] Hippodameia is the noble daughter of Oinomaos whom Pelops seeks to marry. Pelops wins her as his bride after overcoming Oinomaos in the contest.

l: Oinomaos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Oinomaos, king of Pisa and father of Hippodameia, kills thirteen suitors before Pelops overcomes him and wins her.

l: Muse, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Muse, Zeus's divine daughter, sings for silver and tells of great games, keeping a strongest-wingëd dart for Hieron's future glory; she provides triumph songs with the lyre and is asked to come to Aigina to praise Zeus with singers.

l: hill of Kronos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Formerly nameless and snow-sprinkled when Oinomaos was king, the hill was named Hill of Kronos by Herakles at the Olympic sanctuary’s founding.

l: Syracusans, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Syracusans defeat Carthaginians at Himera, fight Hippokrates at Heloros, and under Hieron defeat Etruscans before Cumae, likened to Hellenes’ eastern wars.

l: Hellenes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Hellenes, Pindar’s audience throughout the Greek world, wage war against barbarians in the East, South, and West, including Syracusan victories.

l: Pindar's ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: An ode for Hieron of Syracuse celebrates his horse-race victory and the Olympian games’ preeminence, recalls Pelops as their founder, crowns Hieron in Aeolian strain, and anticipates greater future glory.

l: legend of Pelops' ivory shoulder, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: makes_substitute Pelops' ivory shoulder [for Pelops' fleshly shoulder] The legend claimed that Pelops' ivory shoulder replaced his fleshly shoulder after the gods ate it at Tantalos' table. Pindar refuses to accept the legend because it would make the gods guilty of an infamous act.

l: Graces, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Graces are three goddesses of grace or beauty: Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia. Renowned as queens of Orchomenos and guardians of the Minyai’s ancient race, they give men pleasant things, wisdom, beauty, and fame. They are required by the gods in ruling feasts and dances beside Pythian Apollo, assist victory song, and provide delicious dew for the Psalychidai’s song and fame. Their beauty can make an untrue tale believable.

l: Ixion, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Ixion, a mythical sinner, prospers among the Kronidai, then sheds kindred blood and lusts after Hera, lying with her cloud phantom. Punished by the gods, he is bound without escape to Ixion’s winged wheel, becoming a proclaimer that service merits fair recompense.

l: Theron, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Theron, son of Ainesidamos, brother of Xenokrates of Akragas, and a member of the Emmenidai, traces descent from Polyneikes's son. He wins an Olympian crown in the four-horse chariot-race. Celebrated as a saviour of the state, he supports Akragas and is righteous and god-fearing. Liberal and exceptionally generous toward friends, he gives the Theoxenia for the Dioskouroi, honoring them with hospitality and pious observance, and reaches the furthest bound through fair deeds.

l: the Emmenidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The Emmenidai, ancestors of Theron of Akragas, migrated from Rhodes, first colonized Gela and then Akragas. Especially devoted to and honoring the Dioskouroi with hospitality and pious rites, they receive glory through the Tyndaridai and a lasting treasure of song in Apollo’s valley.

l: Rhodes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Rhodes is a sea-girt island, mythically Aphrodite’s child and Helios’s bride, emerging from the sea under Helios’s rule and receiving gold and handicraft. It is divided among Kameiros, Ialysos, and Lindos, whose confederacy was founded by Argive Dorians.

l: Akragas, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Akragas is a riverside city, called the eye of Sicily, with fields guarded by Zeus, a flock-nourishing stream, a pleasant citadel, and a connection to Persephone. Its people endure long toil to gain wealth, honor, prosperity, and fame, supported by Theron’s noble ancestors. It is celebrated in song for Theron’s Olympian crown, alongside the Emmenidai and Xenokrates, a light of its people. Splendid and beautiful, it finally welcomes Midas and his victory crown.

l: chariot-race victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: occurred_in 476 BC The victory was won by Theron's four-horse chariot, and it is the central occasion for the hymn. Victory is said to release the contestant from the pains of struggle and to bring honor and power.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Herakles is a mighty son of Zeus and Alkmene, also linked with Amphitryon through Zeus’s visit in Amphitryon’s likeness. He is a hero of divinely granted valour and wisdom, whose deeds are continually celebrated, and later a god honored by the immortals. As an infant, he was the target of serpents sent by Hera and strangled them. Teiresias foretold that he would overcome monsters and enemies, fight the giants beside the gods, gain rest from his labors, and marry Hebe. Much of Herakles’ course is defined by great and numerous labors and service to Eurystheus under compulsion. He travels across earth and sea, makes passage safe for ships, sets the Pillars of Herakles as the end of voyaging, wrestles Antaios in Libya, fights giants, and kills Alkyoneus. In war he leads Tirynthian men, joins Telamon against Troy, destroys Troy and Pergamos, and kills the Meropes. At Pylos he contends with Poseidon and is opposed by Poseidon, Phoibos, and Hades. His most enduring foundation is at Pisa and Olympia. After defeating Kleatos and Eurytos and forcing Augeas to pay for service, he gathers host and booty, establishes the Altis and its boundaries, honors Alpheos and the twelve greatest gods, sanctifies Zeus’s altars, and founds the Olympic games. He establishes the fifth-year feast, brings the olive tree from Ister, gives the Dioskouroi charge of the spectacle, and names the Hill of Kronos. After his toils, Herakles marries Hebe and dwells in Olympus, beside Zeus, in peace and divine rest. He remains a recipient of sacrifices and games at Thebes, a friend of Telamon and Aiakos, and a source of strength for mortals facing difficulties.

l: the fifth-year feast, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The fifth-year feast, founded and ordained by Herakles from chief war spoils, is held beside Alpheos at holy steeps.

l: Olympia, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Olympia is a gracious dwelling place of Oinomaos and Pelops at Pisa by the Alpheos, containing Altis, the sacred grove. It is the sacred site of Olympic games, Zeus’s altar, Pelops’s tomb, golden olive-leaves, and crowns for athletic victory. Called the mother of gold-crowned contests and queen of truth, it receives and celebrates triumphs: Psaumis brings honor from it to Kamarina; Agesias, Alkimedon, Epharmostos, Agesidamos, and Ergoteles win there. Its contests glorify Opous and give winners ample glory. The records culminate in its games, founded by Herakles, the first Olympiad, and Pindar’s sight of Agesidamos victorious beside the altar.

l: Semele, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Immortal daughter of Kadmos, cherished on Olympus, bright-filleted queen honored in spring by flute-accompanied hymns despite dying in thunder.

l: Pallas, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Pallas, child of Zeus and queen of steeds, leads Perseus to the Hyperborean folk, then gives Bellerophon Pegasos’s golden bit and directs sacrifice and an altar.

l: Pytho, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Pytho is a place with an old oracle concerning Laïos’ fate, watched over by Leto and her twin children, and a source of Pythian victory crowns and wreaths. It is repeatedly a site of athletic victories: Ergoteles wins twice, Pherenikos wins a race, Telesikrates wins in armour, and Hippokleas wins the boys’ two-stadion race. Apollo is there at sheep-gathering, and Neoptolemos is said to lie beneath its floor.

l: Isthmos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Isthmos is a sea-prisoning, sea-bridging place before the valley of Corinth, sacredly praised with Poseidon. Its games and contests are its chief importance: they grant crowns and victories to the people of Kadmos, Ainesidamos, Herodotos, Melissos, Strepsiades, and Ergoteles, including chariot-racing and pankration prizes.

l: Peleus, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Peleus is a mortal, righteous hero and king, son of Aiakos, associated with the Aiakidai, who rules Phthia and later resides among the blessed in the islands of the blest. He cut and possessed a gigantic spear, captured or conquered Iolkos alone without an army, and delivered it to the Haimones. After rejecting Hippolyte's advances and her false accusation, he was saved by Cheiron from Akastos' ambush. Themis advised that Thetis be given to him; he wrestled with her and held firm, then married her as his sea-bride. Through Thetis, he became a blissful son-in-law of gods and received the prospect of a kingdom for himself and his seed.

l: Achilles, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Achilles is the son of Peleus and Thetis, born in Phthia and linked to Aigina and the Aiakid race. Raised by Cheiron in his cavern and household, he received instruction in reverence for Zeus and parental duty. As a child in Philyra’s house, he killed lions and boars and hunted deer; afterward he became the strongest of men and a warrior superior in battle to Aias. He fought at Troy and elsewhere, killing Telephos on the Mysian plain, Kyknos, Memnon, and Hektor, overcoming Troy’s defenders, and fighting beside Patroklos, whom he urged to remain near him. He died in war by an arrow. Helikonian maidens honored his funeral pyre and tomb, and through his mother’s prayer to Zeus he resides in the islands of the blest.

l: Sun, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Sun is the supreme star, parent of Days, seeing all things and bounding human sight. It is hidden by eclipse, swiftly travels darkness, shines below the blessed dead at night, and is invoked to turn a strange event into good fortune for Thebes.

l: afterlife judgment, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Afterlife judgment judges the dead for sins in Zeus' realm: guilty souls are punished beneath the earth, while virtuous souls, especially those steadfast through repeated lives, receive an unlaborious, tearless life in sunlight at the tower of Kronos. It draws near sorrow or joy and may appear in dreams.

l: wealth, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Wealth is a human possession and source of power when made glorious by noble nature or pure virtue. Joined with good success and fair fame, it supports life’s bloom, brings honor, confidence, and crowns inherited worth. Heaven-sent prosperity shapes a race’s destiny, yet fortune may change. Arkesilas is praised for using great wealth righteously and wisely; gold is called mighty above all else.

l: poetry and song, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: celebrates Theron of Akragas [in a hymn of triumph] The speaker's songs and lyre proclaim Theron's victory, Akragas, and the deeds of heroic and divine figures. The poem presents its arrows or words as meaningful to the wise but requiring interpreters for the multitude, and it contrasts true natural artistry with empty learned chatter.

l: Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Thebes is a seven-gated, divine city associated with Kadmos and the people of Kadmos. In myth it receives Zeus at Amphitryon’s doors, gives birth to Dionysos, and is the land of birth of Heracles through Alkmene; it nurtures Herakles and Iphikles by Dirke’s waters. Its remembered glory includes Teiresias’s wise counsels, Iolaos’s timely deed, the Spartoi, Adrastos’s defeat and return to Argos, and the establishment of a Dorian colony of the men of Lakedaimon. Though this ancient glory is said to sleep through mortal forgetfulness, Thebes remains Pindar’s native state and mother, home of Herodotos, Melissos, and the Kleonymidai. It honors victories with song at the Ismenian shrine, prepares Herakles’s feast, altar-ring, and yearly games on Elektrai, and seeks unimpaired good hap at an eclipse after deliverance from Persian influence and tyrannous oligarchy.

l: future life, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a_subject_of ideas [in Pindar's thought] Pindar's ideas about future life are found especially in the surviving fragments of his Dirges. These ideas seem to have been influenced by Pythagoreanism.

l: Thraenoi (Dirges), The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Thraenoi are dirges surviving only in fragments.

l: Memnon, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Memnon, son of bright Morn, is the chieftain and leader of the Ethiops and Helenos’ fiery cousin. In the war against Troy, he attacks Nestor while Nestor’s chariot is halted by a wounded horse, then fights Achilles hand to hand and is destined to die without returning home.

l: Theoxenia, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a feast [given by Theron in the name of the Dioskouroi] The Theoxenia is a feast given by Theron in the name of the Dioskouroi to the other gods.

l: Dioskouroi, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The Dioskouroi are Kastor and Polydeukes, sons of Tyndareus, invoked at the ode’s beginning and honored by Theron and the Emmenidai through hospitality tables and rites.

l: Kastor, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Kastor, a heroic charioteer, is called son of Zeus and Leto and son of Tyndareus. Twin brother of Polydeukes, he guards Sparta and protects mariners and chariot-race victory. Idas kills him with a bronze spear; Polydeukes appeals to Zeus, and they share immortality between earth and heaven.

l: Polydeukes, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Polydeukes, son of Zeus and Leto, is Kastor’s twin brother, co-protector of mariners, and a guardian of Sparta. After Kastor is struck, Polydeukes kills Lynkeus; Zeus kills Idas. Refusing permanent Olympus, Polydeukes chooses shared immortality with Kastor, alternating beneath earth and in heaven.

l: Amphitryon, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: A charioteer and sword-armed captain, Amphitryon fathers Herakles’ father and rushes to defend the children from serpents, changing from fear to gladness at Herakles’ strength.

l: the olive tree, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The olive tree, brought by Herakles from Ister, was planted as common shade, memorial of Olympic triumphs, and crown for valorous deeds.

l: the Hyperborean folk, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The Hyperborean folk are a blessed, hallowed race who serve Apollo. Free from toil, war, pestilence, old age, and Nemesis, they feast, sing, dance with pipes, and wear golden bay leaves; Perseus once visited as they sacrificed asses to Apollo.

l: Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Apollo is a god, the golden-bowed, flowing-haired son of Zeus and Leto and brother of Artemis, associated with Pytho, Delphi, Sikyon, Kyrene, and the Hyperborean folk. He shares the lyre with the Muses, bestows Muses and song, provides cures, rules the temple at Pytho, and gives oracles, including an infallible prophetic voice to Iamos. As lover and father, he loved Kinyras; fathered Iamos with Euadne, sending Eleutho and the Fates for his birth; rescued his unborn son Asklepios from Koronis's burning corpse after perceiving her union with Ischys, and entrusted him to Cheiron; and carried the lion-fighting Kyrene from Pelion to Libya as his bride, making her queen and fathering Aristaios. He is captain and founder of Kyrene, directs its settlement, gives the Libyan plain to Euphemos's descendants, protects Battos, and drives away lions. He establishes peoples in several places, honors the Ismenian shrine, and is linked to sacred processions and dedications. He brings down Typhon and the king of giants, welcomes Xenarches from Kirrha, and grants victories and glory to Aristomenes, Arkesilas, Chromios, and Hippokleas. He delights in Hyperborean feasts and hymns and in the sound of braying asses.

l: Leto, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: A daughter of Koios and mother of twin children who watch over Pytho, she comes to Delos in childbirth, gives birth there, and beholds her blessed brood.

l: Arcady, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Arcadia is identified as the region where the Iamid clan held hereditary priestly functions. It is also called the nurse of goodly men and is represented through Stymphalos and the Arcadian royal ancestry in the story.

l: the chariot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a Olympic contest [in the spectacle of the games] The chariot-race is the contest in which Theron won his celebrated victory and Olympian crown. The games also included the driving of the nimble car.

l: Theron's Olympian crown, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a crown [won in the chariot-race] Theron's Olympian crown is the subject of the hymn's celebration. It is associated with the pale-gleaming olive glory awarded at the games.

l: the flute, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The flute, devised by Athene to repeat the Gorgons' shrill lament, produces many-headed air through thin-beat bronze and reeds, then becomes a possession of mortal men.

l: Dorian invasion of Peloponnesos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: has_leader Oxylos [one of its leaders] The Dorian invasion of Peloponnesos was said to have been led in part by Oxylos.

l: Oxylos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Oxylos, of Elean descent and living in Aitolia, leads the Dorian invasion and afterward becomes king of Elis.

l: Artemis, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Artemis, an archer maiden, helps Hieron tame colts and honors an unspecified subject as highly as her native Delos.

l: Psaumis, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Psaumis, son of Akron, wins the mule-chariot race at Olympia and receives Pisan olive and an Olympian crown. His victory brings glory to Kamarina. Celebrated for his untiring car and zeal in rearing horses, he honors his father and city through sacrifices and contests. Hospitable, peace-loving, devoted to his city’s welfare, and guileless, he seeks good repute and sufficient wealth; a serene old age with his sons is prayed for.

l: Kamarina, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Kamarina is a new-peopled city, destroyed by Gelo before its restoration and protected by its tutelary nymph. Its citizens, sacred grove, lake, Hipparis-fed sacred channels, twin altars, and five-day games mark it. Psaumis seeks through victory to raise its glory, and Zeus is asked to glorify it.

l: Typhon, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Typhon, a hundred-headed foe of the gods bred in a Kilikian cave, is bound beneath Aitna near Cumae, where he produces fire, smoke, and lava.

l: the mule-chariot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: The mule-chariot-race at Olympia was introduced in 500, won by Psaumis in 452, and abolished in 444, according to Pausanias.

l: Psaumis's Olympian victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Psaumis’s Olympian victory, won in 452 in the mule-chariot race at Olympia, is aided by the Graces and celebrated in song to Zeus. After his return to Kamarina, it brings honor to Psaumis, his father, and the city as a lasting witness to valorous deeds.

l: the ode for Psaumis, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Pindar's ode, among his latest dated works, was written immediately after Psaumis's 452 victory and sung that night beneath the moon by Psaumis's friends returning to give thanks at Zeus's altar.

l: Pythian ix, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: has_introduction an introduction The introduction to Pythian ix is referenced in a footnote.

l: Athene, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Athene, a grey-eyed goddess, is born from Zeus’s head through Hephaistos’ handiwork, crying out as Heaven and Earth tremble. She receives an altar from the sons of Helios and grants the Rhodians mastery of handicraft. After hearing the Gorgon’s death-lament, she devises and creates the flute’s music for mortal men.

l: Athens, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Athens is a city of great fame throughout Hellas, praised as the fairest and most glorious name for songs. It is glorified by Timodemos, linked with Erechtheus and Apollo’s house at divine Pytho, and described through its incensed centre-stone, splendid market-place, and invitation to Olympian gods.

l: Olympian crown, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a wild olive crown The Olympian crown is the proud token of Psaumis’s fame that he consecrates to Kamarina. It represents his victory and is connected with the herald’s public glorification of his father and city.

l: Psaumis' untiring car, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_a car [untiring] Psaumis’ untiring car is offered in connection with the sweet delight of his Olympian victory. It is part of the achievement by which he honors Kamarina.

l: five-day contests of games, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Five-day contests honor six twin altars with ox sacrifices, then horse, mule, chariot, and single-frontlet steed competitions.

l: mules, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: draw Psaumis' untiring car [in the winning race] Mules take part in the five-day contests of games held in honor of the gods. Psaumis wins the mule-chariot race with them.

l: new city, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_built_with wood [brought down the stream of Hipparis] The new city is identified with Kamarina, which had been destroyed by Gelo and restored nine years before the victory. Its rebuilding is associated with bringing the commonwealth from perplexity to light and with constructing steadfast dwellings.

l: citizens of Kamarina, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: form commonwealth The citizens of Kamarina are the people whose commonwealth is brought from perplexity to light as the city is rebuilt. The ode says that successful deeds and wisdom are approved by a person’s own townsfolk.

l: song and poetic fame, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Song and poetic fame are presented as forces that preserve rare, noble, and victorious deeds from obscurity after people die. Through bards’ wisdom, voice, verse, and music, praise comforts, rewards achievement, and carries a clan’s inherited renown forward. The records move from song’s general power to save old glory, to victory praise elevating Timasarchos’s clan, to the Bassids’ continuing fame, to Odysseus’s enlarged honor, and finally to Strepsiades’s newly sung triumph after sorrow.

l: Agesias of Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Agesias, son of Sostratos, was an Iamid descendant, citizen of Syracuse and Stymphalos, joint founder of Syracuse, and treasurer to Zeus’s altar at Pisa; he won Olympia’s mule-chariot race and was praised in a triumphal ode.

l: Iamid clan, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Iamid clan held hereditary priestly functions in Arcadia and Olympia, gaining Hellenic glory through prophetic gifts; Agesias descended from it.

l: Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Syracuse is a great, famous city, associated with Ares, armed men, horses, and the island Ortygia, from which it springs and on which part of it was built. It is the home of Agesias and of Hieron, its ruler and king. From Thebes, the speaker sends or imagines bringing victory song, health, honor, and continuing good fortune to Syracuse, Hieron, and Ortygia.

l: Stymphalos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Stymphalos was Agesias’s other civic home and the place where the ode was sung by a chorus. It is called the mother-city of Arcadia, rich in flocks, and is compared with Syracuse as one of two anchors.

l: mule-chariot race, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_won_by Agesias of Syracuse The mule-chariot race was won by Agesias at Olympia. His mules had already won crowns there, and the poem presents their victory as a deed worthy of song.

l: Olympian victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: belongs_to Agesias of Syracuse The Olympian victory gives Agesias a claim to public praise and makes him treasurer to the prophetic altar of Zeus at Pisa. The ode treats the victory as an achievement won through labor rather than an unthreatening or insignificant deed.

l: the ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: is_sung_by the chorus [in Stymphalos] The ode celebrates Agesias’s victory, ancestry, and civic ties to Syracuse and Stymphalos. It recounts the birth and prophetic destiny of Iamos, praises Hieron and Syracuse, and closes by asking Poseidon to grant safe passage and prosperity.

l: Adrastos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Adrastos belongs to Argos as a returning exile or survivor and is in strife with the sons of Kadmos in an earlier legendary time. As king, he founds and ordains the Pythian games at Sikyon beside Asopos, honoring Phoibos with athletic and chariot contests.

l: Amphiaraos, The Extant Odes of Pindar
s: Amphiaraos is a prophetic figure at Thebes, son of the prophet Oikleus and rival of Adrastos. After fleeing Argos with Adrastos before civil strife, he joins the expedition against seven-gated Thebes, foretells Alkmaion’s nobility and Adrastos’s safe return, and is buried with his steeds when Zeus opens the earth by thunderbolt.
